Foundations: How BI Tools Think About Data

Before you drag a single chart onto a canvas, you need to understand what a dashboard is for, how Power BI and Tableau differ, and how both tools expect data to be shaped. This module covers the two ideas that separate professional dashboards from pretty spreadsheets: the star schema data model and correctly built measures.

A **dashboard** is a single screen that answers a small number of important business questions at a glance, and lets the viewer explore the answer further by clicking. A spreadsheet holds the numbers. A chart shows one view of them. A dashboard combines several connected charts, headline numbers and filters so that a manager can see what is happening, where, and why, in under a minute.

A good dashboard puts the few numbers that matter on one screen and lets the viewer click to explore.

**Power BI** (made by Microsoft) and **Tableau** (owned by Salesforce) are the two business intelligence (BI) tools most often named in data analyst job adverts. Both connect to data, let you build a model and calculations, turn that into interactive visuals, and publish the result so other people can use it in a browser or on the phone app. Once you understand one well, about two thirds of the thinking carries straight over to the other.
The three kinds of dashboard
**Strategic**: for directors and boards. A few headline numbers (revenue, margin, growth against last year), usually checked monthly.
**Operational**: for supervisors running daily work. Today's orders, stock below reorder level, late deliveries. Checked daily or hourly.
**Analytical**: for analysts and managers asking "why". More filters, drill-downs and detail tables to investigate a problem.

Knowing which kind you are building decides almost everything else: how much detail to show, how often the data must refresh, and how many filters to offer. A director who opens a strategic dashboard on her phone between meetings will not use eight slicers. An analyst investigating why Kano sales fell will want them.

Worked example: turning a monthly report into three dashboard questions

For example, Ngozi works for a provisions distributor with four branches: Lagos, Abuja, Kano and Port Harcourt. Each month she spends about two days copying figures from four branch spreadsheets into a 20-page Word report that the managing director rarely reads past page 3.
She asks the managing director what he actually checks on those first three pages. He says: total sales against target, which branch is behind, and which product categories are slipping.

She rewrites these as three dashboard questions: (1) Are we on target this month and year to date? (2) Which branch is furthest behind target, and by how much? (3) Which categories have fallen compared with the same month last year?
She notes the audience: one director, viewing monthly, mostly on his phone. That makes it a strategic dashboard with few filters.
She lists the data needed: sales lines from all four branches, monthly targets per branch, product categories, and at least 13 months of history so that "same month last year" exists.

Ngozi now has a one-page brief that will guide every later decision. The 20 pages shrink to three cards, two charts and one table, and the report can refresh itself instead of taking two days of copying.

Data modelling: fact tables, dimension tables and the star schema
Identify the grain of a table and separate facts from dimensions
Reshape a flat spreadsheet into a star schema
Set one-to-many relationships correctly in Power BI or Tableau
Explain why a separate date table is needed for time comparisons

Most business data arrives as one wide spreadsheet: every row has the date, the branch name, the branch manager, the product, its category, the customer's name, the quantity and the amount. This works for a small table but causes problems in a BI tool: the file grows huge, names get spelt differently in different rows, and calculations become slow and confusing. Both Power BI and Tableau work best when that single sheet is split into a **star schema**.
Facts and dimensions
A **fact table** records events you count or add up: each sale line, each payment, each attendance record. It is long (many rows) and narrow, holding mostly numbers and ID codes.
A **dimension table** describes the things involved in those events: branches, products, customers, dates. It is short (few rows) and holds descriptive text you filter and group by.
The **grain** is what one row of the fact table means, for example "one product on one invoice". Write it down. Mixing grains (some rows per invoice, some per product line) causes double counting.

In a star schema, one long fact table sits in the middle and short dimension tables connect to it.

Relationships and the filter direction

Each dimension connects to the fact table with a **one-to-many relationship**: one branch appears once in the Branch table but many times in the Sales table. The column that links them is a **key**, such as BranchID. In Power BI you create these in Model view by dragging the key from the dimension onto the fact table, and you should see "1" on the dimension side and "*" on the fact side. Keep the cross-filter direction set to **Single**, so that filters flow from dimensions down to facts. Both-direction filtering is sometimes needed, but it can produce surprising totals and should be a deliberate choice, not a default.

In Tableau, you add tables on the Data Source page. In current versions, dragging a second table next to the first creates a **relationship** (a flexible link, shown as a line often called a noodle) instead of a fixed join, and Tableau works out the right level of detail for each chart. You still choose the matching key fields. Use a hard **join** only when you understand that it combines rows into one table, which can duplicate fact rows if the key is not unique.
The duplicate key trap

A dimension key must be unique. If your Product table lists product code P-104 twice (for example once as "Indomie 70g carton" and once as "Indomie carton 70g"), every sale of P-104 can be counted twice when tables are joined, and Power BI will refuse a one-to-many relationship. Remove duplicates in the dimension before you relate it.
Why you need a date table

Comparisons such as "same month last year" or "year to date" need a table holding every single date in the period, with no gaps, plus helper columns such as Year, Month number, Month name and Quarter. In Power BI you can create one with the DAX formula **Date = CALENDAR(DATE(2025,1,1), DATE(2026,12,31))**, add the helper columns, then use **Mark as date table** and relate Date[Date] to the date column in your fact table. Tableau handles dates automatically for most charts, which is one reason beginners find it quicker, but you still need complete history for year-on-year comparisons.
Worked example: splitting a flat sales sheet into a star

For example, Ngozi's distributor exports one sheet per month. Twelve months combined give 18,000 rows with 12 columns: InvoiceNo, Date, Branch, BranchCity, BranchManager, ProductCode, ProductName, Category, CustomerName, Qty, Amount and Profit.
Grain: one row is one product on one invoice. She writes this at the top of her notes.
Fact table Sales keeps InvoiceNo, Date, BranchID, ProductCode, CustomerID, Qty, Amount and Profit: 18,000 rows, 8 columns.

Dimension Branch keeps BranchID, BranchName, City and Manager: 4 rows. Product keeps ProductCode, ProductName and Category: 120 rows after removing duplicates. Customer keeps CustomerID and CustomerName: 950 rows.
She builds a Date table covering 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2026: 730 rows (365 days in each year).
She creates four one-to-many relationships: Branch to Sales, Product to Sales, Customer to Sales and Date to Sales, all single direction.
Check: the branch name used to be stored 18,000 times. Now it is stored 4 times, and a manager's name change is made in one cell.
The model is a clear star with Sales in the middle. Filters on branch, category, customer or month now flow cleanly into every total, and the file is smaller and faster.

A note on spreadsheets that hold **targets**: targets are usually set per branch per month, which is a different grain from sales lines. Keep them in their own small fact table (BranchID, Month, Target) related to the Branch and Date dimensions. Never paste the monthly target onto every sales row, because summing that column would multiply the target by the number of invoices.
Name things for humans

Rename tables and columns to plain words (Sales, Branch, Product; Amount, not AMT_NGN_X). Hide key columns such as BranchID from report view so that viewers only see fields they should drag onto charts.

A dashboard is only as trustworthy as its calculations. The most common errors in BI work are not chart choices but numbers that are calculated at the wrong level: a margin averaged instead of recomputed, a total that ignores a filter, a growth rate divided by zero. This lesson teaches the core calculation habits in both tools.

Behind every bar is a measure; get the measure right and every chart that uses it is right.

If the answer must change when the viewer clicks a filter, it should be a measure.

In Power BI, create measures with **New measure** and give them clear names. Start with simple base measures, then build others on top of them. This keeps every formula short and means a correction in one place fixes every visual.
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Total Profit = SUM(Sales[Profit])
Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])  (DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error when sales are zero)
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))  (needs the marked date table from the last lesson)
Sales Growth % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
Lagos Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Branch[City] = "Lagos")  (CALCULATE changes the filter for this one measure)

**CALCULATE** is the most important DAX function. It evaluates a measure after changing the filters around it. When a visual shows March 2026 for Abuja, the measure Total Sales is calculated only for those rows. Sales LY uses CALCULATE to shift the date filter back one year while keeping the Abuja filter. Learn to say in words what filter each measure applies, and you will understand most of DAX.
The same ideas in Tableau

In Tableau, fields from your data are sorted into **dimensions** (things you group by, usually shown in blue as discrete) and **measures** (numbers you aggregate, usually shown in green as continuous). Dragging a measure onto a shelf automatically applies SUM. You create new logic with **Analysis > Create Calculated Field**.
Profit Ratio: **SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])**. Aggregating first, then dividing, gives the correct margin at any level.
Writing **[Profit] / [Sales]** instead computes a ratio on every row, and Tableau then sums or averages those row ratios, which is wrong for a margin.

First Purchase Date: **{FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])}**. This LOD expression finds each customer's first order date regardless of other filters on the view, which lets you count new versus returning customers.
Tableau has quick table calculations (right-click a measure, Quick Table Calculation) for running totals, percent of total and year-on-year growth.
Worked example: the average-of-ratios mistake
For example, Ngozi's dashboard shows profit margin by branch. Lagos sold ₦4,000,000 with ₦600,000 profit. Kano sold ₦1,000,000 with ₦300,000 profit. The director asks for the combined margin.
Wrong method: average the two margins. (15% + 30%) ÷ 2 = 22.5%.
Right method: add first, then divide. Total profit 600,000 + 300,000 = ₦900,000. Total sales 4,000,000 + 1,000,000 = ₦5,000,000.
In Power BI, Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales]) gives 18% in the total row automatically. In Tableau, SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) gives 18%.

The correct combined margin is 18%, not 22.5%. Reporting 22.5% would overstate the business's margin by 4.5 percentage points, because Kano's small sales were given the same weight as Lagos's large sales.
Worked example: year-on-year growth
For example, the Abuja branch sold ₦12,400,000 in March 2026 and ₦10,000,000 in March 2025.
Sales LY for March 2026 returns ₦10,000,000.
The card shows +24% for Abuja in March. For a new branch with no sales last year, DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error, which is the honest answer.
Filter context in plain words

Every number in a visual is calculated inside a **filter context**: the set of filters coming from the row or bar it sits in, the slicers on the page, and any filters on the visual or report. When the director clicks Kano on a bar chart, every measure on the page is recalculated for Kano only. Measures are powerful precisely because they respond to this context. Calculated columns do not: they were worked out once, row by row, when the data loaded. That is why a calculated column called Margin, averaged in a visual, gives the wrong answer, while a Profit Margin measure gives the right one at every level.

A good habit is to keep all measures in one place, for example a table called Measures in Power BI or a folder in Tableau's Data pane, and to set their number format once (percentage with one decimal place, or naira with no decimals). Then every visual that uses them shows consistent numbers without extra formatting work.
Test every measure in a plain table first

Before putting a new measure on a chart, drop it into a simple table next to branch and month, and check two or three values with a calculator against the source data. This takes five minutes and catches most mistakes.

Recorded steps, not manual edits

In Power BI, choose **Get data**, pick your file, then **Transform data** to open the **Power Query editor**. Every change you make, such as removing rows or renaming a column, is recorded in the **Applied Steps** list on the right. Next month, you drop the new file into the same folder and click **Refresh**: all the steps run again. Behind the scenes Power Query writes these steps in a language called M, which you can view in the Advanced Editor but rarely need to type.

In Tableau Public, the Data Source page lets you use the **Data Interpreter** (which detects title rows and headers in Excel sheets), rename fields, change data types, split columns and pivot columns into rows. For heavier cleaning, Tableau offers a separate tool called Tableau Prep, which records steps as a flow. For practice, the Data Source page is usually enough.

**Slicers and filters**: In Power BI, a slicer visual for Month or Branch filters the whole page. In Tableau, show a filter card by right-clicking a field on the Filters shelf and choosing Show Filter, then use Apply to Worksheets so it affects every sheet on the dashboard.

**Cross-filtering**: In Power BI, clicking a bar filters the other visuals on the page by default; use Format > Edit interactions to switch this off where it confuses. In Tableau, add a **filter action** (Dashboard > Actions) or click the filter icon on a sheet to use it as a filter.
**Drill-down**: put Year, Quarter and Month (or Region, State, Branch) in a hierarchy so viewers can click down a level. Tell them it exists; many viewers never discover it.
**Tooltips**: show extra context on hover or tap, such as last year's value or the target, without adding another chart.
**Reset**: give viewers a clear way back to the default view (a bookmark button in Power BI, or a Revert option in Tableau) so they do not get lost.

A dashboard that shows one wrong number loses the viewer's trust in every other number on it. Quality assurance (QA) is the set of checks you run before anyone else sees the dashboard, and again after every major change. It has three parts: are the **numbers** right, does the **interaction** work, and is the **design** honest?
A person checking data on a screen with a tick mark
Reconcile your totals with the source before anyone makes a decision from them.
1. Reconcile the numbers

**Reconciliation** means comparing your dashboard's totals with an independent, trusted figure, such as the month-end total in the accounting system, the bank statement, or the figure finance reported. Pick at least three checks: the grand total, one branch, and one month. Differences must be explained, not ignored.
Worked example: finding a ₦450,000 difference
For example, Ngozi's dashboard shows total sales for June of ₦48,350,000. The finance team's ledger shows ₦47,900,000.
Difference: 48,350,000 minus 47,900,000 = ₦450,000. The dashboard is too high.
She filters to each branch in turn. Lagos, Abuja and Kano match finance exactly. Port Harcourt is ₦450,000 too high.
In a table of Port Harcourt invoices for June, she sorts by invoice number and finds three invoices each appearing twice, each worth ₦150,000.
Check: 3 × 150,000 = ₦450,000, exactly the difference.
Cause: the branch exported mid-month and again at month end, and both files sat in the raw folder.
Fix: she adds a Remove Duplicates step on InvoiceNo and ProductCode in Power Query, refreshes, and the total becomes ₦47,900,000.
The dashboard now reconciles with finance. She records the cause and fix in her QA log, and adds a rule to the handover note: one export file per branch per month.
2. Test the interaction
Click every slicer value, including "Select all" and a value with no data. Does every visual update, and do blanks show sensibly instead of errors?
Click a bar in each chart. Do the other visuals cross-filter as intended?
Drill down and back up every hierarchy.
Check that totals in tables equal the sum of their rows, especially for ratio measures.

Open the phone layout on an actual phone, on mobile data, and note how long it takes to load. In Power BI, View > Performance analyzer shows which visuals are slow; Tableau has a performance recording feature for the same purpose.
3. Check the design is honest
Honest chart checks
Bar axes start at zero
Same scale on compared charts
Months in calendar order
Units shown on every axis
Colour means one thing
Each check prevents a chart from exaggerating or hiding a difference, even by accident.

A bar chart whose axis starts at ₦40 million instead of zero can make a ₦2 million difference look like a doubling. Two charts side by side with different scales invite wrong comparisons. Line charts may use a non-zero axis when showing small changes over time, but label it clearly. Use colour consistently: if amber means "below target" on one chart, it must not mean "Kano" on another.
4. Document it
Write a short **data dictionary** and **handover note** in your docs folder. It turns your dashboard from something only you understand into something an organisation can rely on.
Item
What to write

Each file or system, who provides it, how it is exported, and how often
Measures
Name, plain-English definition and formula, for example Profit Margin = total profit divided by total sales
Refresh
Manual or scheduled, when, and who presses refresh if manual
Known limits
For example, Port Harcourt data starts in March 2025, so year-on-year is blank before March 2026
Owner and version
Who maintains it, the version number and date, and a short change log
5. Ask a real user to test it

Finally, sit with one real viewer, ideally the person who will use the dashboard most, and watch them use it without helping. Ask them to answer the three brief questions using the dashboard alone. Note where they hesitate, what they click that does nothing, and any word they do not understand. Common findings are filters hidden at the edge of the screen, abbreviations such as "YoY" or "PY" that need spelling out, and numbers without units. Fix these before release, then record the session in your QA log.

Schedule QA again whenever the data source changes, a new measure is added, or the client reports a surprising number. A quick monthly check that the grand total still matches the source catches problems early, before a director quotes a wrong figure in a meeting.

Use a simple sheet with columns: date, check performed, expected value, dashboard value, pass or fail, action taken. Clients and employers value this evidence, and you can show an anonymised version in your portfolio.

Most dashboard projects that fail do so before any chart is built: the analyst built what she assumed was needed, the data could not be accessed, or the finished dashboard could not be shared with the right people. A good **discovery** meeting prevents all three. Plan for 45 to 60 minutes, take notes, and send a written summary afterwards.

Sharing safely

**Power BI service**: publish from Desktop to a workspace, then share the report or an app with named colleagues. Sharing with others generally needs a paid licence for each user, or a capacity licence held by the organisation. Check what the client already has before promising.
**Publish to web (Power BI)**: creates a public link anyone can open. Microsoft warns that it is for public data only. Never use it for client or staff data.
**Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server**: private sharing for organisations with Tableau licences.
**Tableau Public**: free, but everything saved there is public. Use only for public or invented data, for example in your portfolio.
**Static export**: a PDF or image of the dashboard sent by email or WhatsApp. Not interactive, but sometimes the simplest safe option for a small client.

**Row-level security (RLS)** lets one dashboard show different rows to different viewers. In Power BI you create roles in Desktop (Modeling > Manage roles) with a DAX filter, such as Branch[City] = "Kano", test them with View as, then assign people to each role in the Power BI service. Tableau achieves the same with user filters or data policies on Tableau Cloud or Server. RLS only works when the report is shared through the service; it does not protect a file you email.
Personal data and the law

The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees it. In practice: collect only the columns you need, remove or mask names and phone numbers where totals are enough, store client files on encrypted or password-protected devices, delete copies when the project ends, and put these promises in writing. Never send login details or data exports over open WhatsApp groups.

Data: monthly Google Sheets from each state, about 2,400 member rows in total, including members' names and phone numbers.
Refresh: monthly is enough. A coordinator will upload sheets to a shared folder by the 5th of each month.

Access: each coordinator should see only her own state, and the donor should see only totals, no names. Halima proposes row-level security by state and removing names and phone numbers from the model entirely, using member ID only.
Sharing: the NGO already uses Microsoft 365, so she confirms in writing which Power BI licences the four viewers will need before quoting.
Halima sends a one-page summary. The manager corrects one point (savings targets are per group, not per member), confirms the rest, and Halima can now scope and price the work accurately.

Dashboard projects are easy to underprice. The visible part, the charts, takes the least time. Data access, cleaning, reconciliation and revisions take the most, and clients cannot see that work. A clear estimate and a tightly written proposal protect both you and the client.

Then decide your hourly rate from your experience level, your local market, and what similar freelancers charge on the platforms and networks you use. For example, Chioma is quoting the distributor's dashboard: four branch data sources, a target sheet, two report pages (director summary and branch detail), a phone layout, and one training session. She uses an illustrative rate of ₦15,000 per hour.

Contingency of 15% for unknown data problems: 780,000 × 0.15 = ₦117,000. Subtotal: ₦897,000. She rounds to ₦900,000.

Optional monthly support: refresh checks and up to 6 hours of small changes, 6 × ₦15,000 = ₦90,000 per month.

Chioma quotes a fixed ₦900,000 for the defined scope, with a clear payment schedule and an optional ₦90,000 monthly support plan. Data cleaning is 16 of 52 hours, about 31% of the effort, which she explains to the client.

What the proposal must say

**Data sources included**, by name, and the client's duty to provide exports or access by a set date.
**Deliverables**: number of pages, phone layout yes or no, number of measures or KPIs, training sessions, documentation.
**Revision rounds**: for example, two rounds of changes on the first draft. Further rounds are charged.
**Not included**: for example, new data sources, extra pages, licence costs, data entry, fixing the client's source systems.
**Timeline, price, payment schedule** and what happens if client data arrives late.
**Data handling**: how you will store, protect and delete their data.
Payment safety

Take a deposit before starting and receive payments into your registered business or personal account through a traceable channel such as a bank transfer or a payment link from a provider like Paystack. Be wary of overseas "clients" who send more than the agreed amount and ask for a refund of the difference; this is a common overpayment scam. Never share your banking passwords or one-time codes with anyone.
Common reasons dashboard quotes go wrong
The client's data is spread across many Excel files with different layouts each month, so cleaning takes far longer than estimated. Ask for three months of samples, not one.
Nobody on the client side owns the data, so exports arrive late. Name the client contact responsible in the proposal.
Licences were not discussed, and the client expected free sharing with 20 staff. Raise licence needs during discovery, and state that licence costs are paid by the client.
The "final" dashboard keeps changing because stakeholders were not consulted early. Agree who approves the draft, and limit revision rounds.

Put your estimate in a small spreadsheet with one row per phase, columns for estimated and actual hours, and a notes column. After each project, compare the two. If data cleaning took 24 hours instead of 16, raise that phase in your next estimate. Within a few projects your quotes will become reliable.

Hours set your minimum price. Value can justify more. If the distributor's analyst currently spends about two days each month on a manual report, the dashboard frees roughly 24 working days a year. Explain that in the proposal in plain terms. Avoid promising specific financial gains you cannot measure; describe time saved and faster decisions instead.

Employers and clients hiring for Power BI or Tableau work want proof that you can take messy data to a trustworthy, usable dashboard. A small portfolio of well-explained projects is more convincing than a long list of tutorials completed. This lesson shows you what to build, how to present it, and how to plan the next 90 days.
A portfolio website showing several project cards
Three well-explained dashboards show more skill than twenty unexplained screenshots.
Three projects, three skills
**Project 1, business sales dashboard**: a star schema with a date table, measures including margin and year-on-year growth, and a target comparison. Shows modelling and DAX or calculated fields.
**Project 2, messy data rescue**: start from a genuinely messy public dataset and document every cleaning step, row count and reconciliation. Shows Power Query or Tableau data skills and QA.

**Project 3, public interest or NGO dashboard**: use open data, for example from a national statistics office, the World Bank or an open data portal, with a clear story for a non-technical audience. Shows communication and design.
Never put client data in your portfolio

Use only public, invented or fully anonymised data with the client's written permission. Tableau Public and Power BI's Publish to web make everything visible to anyone. For client work, show screenshots with names, figures and logos removed or replaced.
Write a short case study for each

Under each dashboard, write 150 to 250 words: the business question, the audience, the data and how you cleaned it, two design decisions and why you made them (for example, "I used a sorted bar chart of variance instead of a map because the director needs to see which branch is furthest behind"), and what you checked during QA. This shows thinking, not just button clicking. Tableau Public lets you publish interactive work to a public profile; for Power BI work, share a short screen recording and screenshots, or Publish to web only for fully public data.
Certification routes

Microsoft offers the **Power BI Data Analyst Associate** certification, earned by passing **exam PL-300**. Microsoft Learn has a free learning path for it, and the exam is paid. Tableau also offers certifications, listed on Tableau's learning and certification pages; check the current names, prices and formats there before choosing, as they change. A certificate helps you pass CV screening, but your portfolio is what convinces in an interview.

Weeks 5 to 8 (32 hours): build Project 3, set up her Tableau Public profile and a simple portfolio page, update her LinkedIn headline and CV with her three projects.

By day 90 Amaka has three documented dashboards, a public profile, 15 applications and 10 pitches tracked, and a clear next step. Each week has a number she can tick off, so progress is visible even before the first offer arrives.

Where to look for work: data analyst and BI roles in banks, fintechs, telecoms, FMCG companies, consultancies and NGOs; remote contract work through freelance platforms and your LinkedIn network; and small local businesses and associations that still report from scattered spreadsheets. Start with the people and sectors you already know. Your first paid project often comes from someone who trusts you, not from a stranger online.

A dashboard is a single screen that answers a few important business questions at a glance, joining charts, headline numbers and filters.
The viewer can click to explore, and see what is happening, where, and why, in under a minute.
Power BI and Tableau are the two tools most named in data analyst job adverts. Learn one well, and about two thirds of the thinking carries over.
This module teaches what separates a professional dashboard from a pretty spreadsheet: a sound data model and correct measures.
Know your audience
For directors and boards. A few headline numbers like revenue and margin, usually checked monthly.
For supervisors running daily work. Today's orders, low stock, late deliveries. Checked daily or hourly.
For analysts asking why. More filters, drill-downs and detail tables to investigate a problem.
First, decide which kind of dashboard you are building, because it decides almost everything else.
A strategic dashboard is for directors. A few headline numbers, usually checked monthly.
An operational dashboard is for supervisors running daily work, such as today's orders and late deliveries. It is checked daily or even hourly.
An analytical dashboard is for people asking why, so it has more filters, drill-downs and detail.
Step by step
Write the brief before you build
Every visual must answer a question. If it answers none, leave it out.
Ask the user what they actually check
Turn that into three dashboard questions
Note the audience and how often they view
List the data each question needs
Professionals start with a short written brief, not with the tool.
For example, Ngozi spent about two days a month on a 20-page report that her managing director rarely read past page 3. So she asked him what he actually checks.
She turned his answer into three questions. Are we on target? Which branch is furthest behind? Which categories have fallen compared with last year?
She noted the audience: one director, viewing monthly, mostly on his phone. That makes it a strategic dashboard with few filters.
Then she listed the data needed, including at least 13 months of history, so that same month last year exists.
Here is the rule. Every visual you add must answer one of your questions. If it answers none, it does not go on the page.
The star schema
Fact tables and dimension tables
Fact table
Events you count or add up
Long: many rows
Mostly numbers and ID codes
Example: each sale line
Dimension table
Describes the things involved
Short: few rows
Text you filter and group by
Example: branches, products, dates
Most business data arrives as one wide sheet, which gets huge and slow in a BI tool. So you split it into a star schema.
A fact table records events you count or add up, such as each sale line.
A dimension table describes the things involved: branches, products, customers and dates.
In Ngozi's model, the branch name used to be stored 18,000 times. Now it is stored 4 times.
Model rules
Five rules for a sound model
Write down the grain of the fact table
Keep every dimension key unique
One-to-many, single direction filters
Build a complete date table
Keep targets in their own small table
Write down the grain: what one row of the fact table means, such as one product on one invoice. Mixing grains causes double counting.
Keep every dimension key unique. If product code P-104 appears twice with two spellings, its sales can be counted twice.
Link each dimension to the fact table with a one-to-many relationship, and keep the filter direction single, so filters flow from dimensions down to facts.
Comparisons like year to date need a date table with every date and no gaps.
And keep targets in their own table. Pasting the monthly target onto every sales row multiplies it by the number of invoices.
Calculations
A calculated column is worked out once, row by row, when the data loads. Use it to group or filter, like a price band per product.
A measure is calculated when a visual asks for it, so it responds to every filter. Use measures for totals and ratios, like profit margin.
Worked example
The average-of-ratios mistake
For example, Ngozi's director asks for the combined profit margin of Lagos and Kano.
Lagos sales
Lagos profit
Kano sales
Kano profit
Here is the most common calculation mistake. Ngozi's director asks for the combined profit margin of two branches.
Lagos sold 4,000,000 naira with 600,000 naira profit. That is a 15% margin.
Kano sold 1,000,000 naira with 300,000 naira profit. That is 30%.
The wrong method averages the two margins and gets 22.5%.
The right method adds first, then divides. 900,000 divided by 5,000,000 is 18%.
Ratios must be sum divided by sum, never an average of ratios. Test every new measure in a plain table with a calculator before you chart it.
Key points
Remember
Write questions and audience before you build
Facts hold events; dimensions hold descriptions
Unique keys, single direction, full date table
Measures for anything that must respond to filters
Ratios: sum divided by sum, never averaged
To remember. Write your questions and audience down first. Facts hold events, dimensions hold descriptions.
Keep keys unique and your date table complete. Use measures for anything that must respond to filters, and calculate ratios as sum divided by sum.

Experienced analysts say most of a dashboard project is spent preparing data. Exports arrive with title rows, mixed spellings, blank rows and numbers stored as text.

Step by step
The standard cleaning checklist
Never clean the raw file by hand. Let recorded steps do it.
In Power BI, open the Power Query editor. Every change is recorded in Applied Steps, and runs again when you click Refresh. In Tableau, use the Data Source page and the Data Interpreter.
First, remove title rows and blank rows.
Use the first row as headers, and set each column's data type, so amounts are numbers, not text.
Trim spaces and fix spellings, so Abuja, ABUJA and Abj become one value.
Remove true duplicates, such as the same invoice line exported twice.
Unpivot month columns into rows, so viewers can filter by month. For example, Tunde turned 40 categories by 12 month columns into 480 rows.
Then check. Tunde's editor showed 480 rows, and the grand total still matched the original sheet, so nothing was lost.
The rule: never fix the raw file by hand. Next month the same problems return. Keep raw files untouched and let recorded steps do the cleaning.
Safety first
If a column does not answer a dashboard question, remove it in your first cleaning step.
Never upload files with personal data to Tableau Public. Everything saved there is public.
Do not email raw exports through personal accounts.
Customer names, phone numbers and account details fall under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.
If a column is not needed to answer the dashboard questions, remove it in your very first cleaning step.
Never upload files containing personal data to Tableau Public, because everything saved there can be seen by anyone.
And do not email raw exports through personal accounts.
Layout
Wireframe first, then build
Headline KPI cards across the top
Main trend or comparison in the middle
Detail tables at the bottom
Filters in one consistent place
Two or three colours only
A wireframe is a rough sketch showing where each card, chart and filter will sit, and which question each one answers. It takes ten minutes and saves hours.
People scan from the top left, so put the headline numbers, called KPI cards, across the top.
Put the main trend or comparison chart in the middle, and detail tables at the bottom.
Keep filters in one place, and use two or three colours: a neutral one, a highlight, and red or amber only for real warnings.
Then show it to someone for five seconds. If they cannot tell you the main message, simplify.
Chart choice
Match the chart to the question
Good choice
Compare: sorted horizontal bar
Trend: line chart, months in order
Target: bar with a target line
Exact values: table or matrix
3D bars
Pies with many tiny slices
Gauges showing one number
To compare branches, use a sorted horizontal bar chart. For a trend over months, a line chart. For actual against target, a bar with a target line. For exact values, a table.
Avoid 3D bars, pie charts with many tiny slices, gauges that take space to show one number, and maps used just for decoration.
Worked example
Finding a 450,000 naira difference
For example, Ngozi reconciles her June dashboard total with the finance team's ledger.
Dashboard total, June
Finance ledger, June
Difference, all Port Harcourt
Each duplicated invoice (3)
Reconciliation means comparing your totals with a trusted figure, such as the accounting system. Check the grand total, one branch and one month.
Ngozi's dashboard shows 48,350,000 naira for June. Finance shows 47,900,000. The dashboard is 450,000 naira too high.
She filters branch by branch. Only Port Harcourt is off.
Sorting its invoices, she finds three invoices each appearing twice, each worth 150,000 naira. Three times 150,000 is exactly 450,000. The branch had exported twice.
She adds a Remove Duplicates step, refreshes, and the total becomes 47,900,000 naira. It now matches finance.
Every difference must be explained, not ignored.
Before you share
Run these honest chart checks. A bar axis that starts at 40 million naira instead of zero can make a small difference look huge.
Bars start at zero. Compared charts share a scale. Months in order. Units on every axis. And if amber means below target, it means only that.

Five areas to cover every time
Decisions: what will this help you decide?
Audience: who views it, how often, what device?
Data sources: where does each number live?
Refresh: monthly, weekly or daily?
Access and privacy: who may see what?
Plan 45 to 60 minutes, take notes, and cover five areas.
Decisions. What will this dashboard help you decide? A dashboard that changes no decision will be abandoned.
Audience. Who will view it, how often, and on what device? That decides the design and the phone layout.
Data sources. Where does each number live today, and who can export it? Ask for a sample export before you quote.
Refresh. How fresh must the data be, and who will press refresh?
Access and privacy. Who may see what, and does the data include personal details?
Afterwards, send a written summary and ask the client to correct it.
Safety first
Sharing safely and legally
Publish to web and Tableau Public are for public data only. Never use them for client or staff data.
Shows each viewer only their own rows, but only when shared through the service, not in an emailed file.
Collect only the columns you need, mask names and phones, protect devices, delete copies at the end.
Publish to web in Power BI, and Tableau Public, make your work visible to anyone. Use them for public data only, never for client or staff data.
Row-level security lets one dashboard show each viewer only their own rows, such as a coordinator seeing only her state. It works only when shared through the service, not on a file you email.

The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone handling personal data. Collect only what you need, mask names and phone numbers, protect your devices, and delete copies when the project ends.
Never send logins or data exports over open WhatsApp groups.
